prompt: What makes a group of customers a segment rather than a chart?

choices.text: It was found by an algorithm rather than written by a person who knows the business
choices.why: Rules written by people make segments too.

choices.text: It has more than a thousand customers
choices.why: Size matters, but it is not the definition.
Seven named groups emailed identically are still a chart.

prompt: Two segments would receive exactly the same offer. What does the lesson say about them?

choices.why: Reporting is a chart's job; a segment exists to be treated differently.

choices.text: Merge them only if they are both smaller than a few hundred customers each
choices.why: Size is a separate test from whether the action differs.

prompt: What can clustering do that rules like RFM cannot?

choices.text: Explain each group in one sentence

choices.why: Its centres move with the data.

choices.text: Choose the number of groups by itself, without anybody having to decide how many there should be

prompt: Why is the recency score reversed, with the smallest recency getting a 5?

choices.text: Recency is measured backwards in time
choices.why: Every measure here looks back; the score just follows what is good.

choices.text: pandas sorts dates in descending order by default, so the labels come out reversed
choices.why: The labels are written reversed on purpose.

prompt: Why turn recency, frequency and spend into quintile scores?

choices.why: Outliers land in the top or bottom fifth; they are not removed.
Right. Days, orders and reais become 1 to 5.

choices.text: Because RFM requires exactly five levels, as defined in the original method from the 1990s
choices.why: Three levels are fine, as the lesson says.

prompt: A quarter of customers ordered within the last 6 days. Why does the program rank them before cutting?

choices.text: Tied values do not split into five equal groups, so each customer needs a distinct position first
choices.why: Right. The cost is that equal recencies can get neighbouring scores.

choices.text: Ranking removes customers who ordered on the same day as somebody else

choices.why: It accepts any numbers; ties are the problem.

prompt: What share of the year's spend did the champions account for, in per cent?
Why are the 'at risk' customers the most valuable target for a win-back offer?

choices.text: They ordered most recently, so a reminder would reach them while they still remember the boxes
They had a habit and lost it
choices.why: Right. There is something to win back.

prompt: 'Lost' and 'new or occasional' both ordered about four times in the year. What separates them?

choices.text: The channel that brought them, which RFM reads from the customer table

choices.why: Right. One ordered recently, the other long ago.

prompt: Why are the segment rules written beside the report?

choices.text: So a segment keeps meaning the same thing next month and for the next analyst who reads it
For legal reasons, since customer segments are personal data that must be documented

prompt: Why does the program scale the three features before k-means?

choices.text: Otherwise reais would outweigh days just by being larger

choices.why: Scaled values are not limited to 0 and 1.

choices.text: To remove customers with no orders
To make the clusters come out in the same order every time the program is run

prompt: Inertia falls from 6,793 with two clusters to 2,084 with six. Why not pick six?

choices.text: Six is too many for scikit-learn

choices.why: Lower is tighter; it just keeps falling.

choices.text: Six clusters have a negative silhouette
Inertia falls with every extra cluster, so it cannot choose k alone
choices.why: Right. More centres are always closer.

prompt: The silhouette is highest for two clusters, yet the lesson keeps four. Why?

choices.text: Four are nearly as clean and match the actions Panela has
choices.why: Right. The business chooses k within what the data allows.

choices.text: k-means always needs an even number of clusters
